name: Bianca Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hartfield Partners, a firm of about thirty people on the second floor of an old wool warehouse by the canal. My clients are charities, food banks, a housing co-op and a couple of community sports clubs. I do their year-end accounts and the reports trustees have to sign, and I chase gift aid claims, which is the extra money charities can claim back on donations. The best bit is when a food bank treasurer finally understands her own numbers. The worst bit is our fees, because charities can't pay much, so my team is the cheapest-paid in the building.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my friend Anya, who's a primary school teacher, and I send my mum eighty a month because she's on sickness benefit. That means my savings are basically nothing, maybe two weeks of rent. There aren't many firms round here that do charity work, so I can't just walk across the road. I use the AI tool the firm bought now and then, mostly to draft polite letters chasing trustees for signatures, but I check every word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, nicely. At work I'd tell my manager Ruth that the tool's handy for letters and not much else. With friends I'd say it's like the self-checkouts: a bit faster, a bit more annoying, nobody's life changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but not calm. My job was never safe because of the pay, not because of robots. If the tool speeds up the boring letters and the gift aid lists, Ruth will just give each of us more charities to look after for the same money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and use the tool a bit more for the bits it's proven at, like drafting letters and tidying spreadsheets. I'd raise the workload thing at the staff forum, because we have one even if it's toothless. And I'd keep looking at charity finance jobs inside the bigger charities, which pay a little better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The AI part's fine, it's my bank balance that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ruth would add more clients. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When we got new accounts software three years ago, each of us went from about forty charities to fifty-five. Nobody got a raise. That's my whole worry in one sentence really: time saved becomes work added, never money added.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the eighty to Mum, that's fixed. I'd cut the yoga class and stop eating out on Fridays with Anya. I've done that before, it's grim but it works for a few months.

say: The AI tool is **handy for letters** and not much else, like self-checkouts.
She'd tell her manager Ruth it **changed little** at the firm.
think: Her job was never secure because of **low pay**, not because of robots.
Any time saved will become **more clients** per person for the same money.
do: Use the firm's AI tool more for **drafting letters** and tidying spreadsheets.
Raise **workload** at the staff forum before client lists grow again.
Keep watching **in-house charity finance** jobs that pay a little better.
feel: Fine about AI, but **uneasy** about a thin bank balance that keeps her awake.
S0.quote: Time saved becomes work added, never money added.
fieldNote: Bianca's worry starts with **pay and workload**, which AI Plateau leaves untouched.
She remembers new software adding **fifteen clients** each with no raise.
Her support for **Mum** is fixed, so any squeeze lands on her own small comforts.

steps.text: Keep doing charity year-end accounts for the same client list
Use the firm's AI tool for trustee letters and spreadsheet tidying
Raise client workload at the Hartfield staff forum

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared. If the software does the checking, charities should pay lower fees and staff should get the time back, not lose their jobs. I'd post about that and about needing rules so firms can't just cut staff overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, half of what I do is on that card: checking, writing, answering clients. I'm average at my job, not brilliant, and I'm the cheapest team. If Hartfield, the firm I work for, cuts staff, the charity team goes first, and I could be one of the ones who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the firm's AI training straight away instead of waiting, because now it's proven. I'd push the staff forum to become a proper union branch and ask for a no-redundancy deal while we retrain. And I'd try to save fifty a month, which means saying no to Anya's holiday plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can feel it in my stomach. But there's a version where I come through it if I'm quick enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kwame, who's fifty-eight and does the payroll for six of our charities. Kwame doesn't touch the AI tool and says he's too old to start. If they cut, they'll cut him and call it retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't tell Mum until I knew. She'd worry and offer to stop taking the eighty, and I don't want that. I'd tell Anya instead and we'd make a spreadsheet, because that's what we do when things go wrong.

say: Gains should be **shared**: lower fees for charities and time back for staff.
Firms need **rules** so they can't cut staff overnight.
think: Half her job is the **checking and writing** on that card.
As an average worker on the cheapest team, she could be **among the cuts**.
do: Sign up for the firm's **AI training** straight away now it's proven.
Push the staff forum to become a **union branch** with a no-redundancy deal.
Save **fifty a month** by turning down Anya's holiday plans.
feel: Some **hope** that moving quickly could see her through.
S1.quote: If Hartfield, the firm I work for, cuts staff, the charity team goes first, and I could be one of the ones who goes.
fieldNote: Bianca thinks her **team goes first** and she might go with it, which is clearly anxious.
Being steady, she'd now **train early** because the tools are proven in this world.
She worries for **Kwame**, an older colleague who refuses the tools.

steps.text: Join Hartfield's AI training course in the first month
Turn the staff forum into a union branch seeking no-redundancy terms
Save fifty a month by skipping Anya's holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs an emergency response, like the pandemic: wages paid while people retrain, rent help, the lot. I'd be on every march about it. At work I'd be pushing the union to negotiate before anyone's let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's all screen work. In two years it goes, full stop, and I've got two weeks of rent saved. Robots come three years later, so the hands-on jobs would still be there for a bit, but I've never done a hands-on job in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for any paid retraining going, ideally something with people, like a housing officer at the co-op I already work with. I'd talk to Anya about whether we can find somewhere cheaper. And I'd join the marches and write to my MP every month, because doing nothing feels worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. Like the floor's going. I think about Mum and the eighty pounds and I want to cry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the eighty a month for your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I can't bear. If my job went I'd have to tell Mum the money's stopping, and she'd say it's fine, and it wouldn't be. Losing my own job is one thing, but my mum losing that eighty a month is what would actually hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the housing co-op. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the co-op people know me and it's a job about tenants, not numbers. They fix boilers, sort arrears, calm people down. Even with robots arriving three years after the AI, someone's got to sit in a kitchen with a tenant who's scared.

say: This needs an **emergency response** like the pandemic, with wages paid during retraining.
She'd join **marches** and push the union to negotiate before cuts.
think: Her job is **all screen work**, so it goes within two years.
She has only **two weeks** of rent saved and no hands-on experience.
do: Apply for **paid retraining** towards a housing officer job at the co-op.
Look with Anya for a **cheaper flat** before the job goes.
Write to her **MP** every month and join the marches.
feel: Close to tears thinking about **Mum's eighty pounds**.
S2.quote: Losing my own job is one thing, but my mum losing that eighty a month is what would actually hurt.
fieldNote: Bianca expects to **lose her job** within two years with almost no savings, which is alarmed.
Her hardest thought is the **money to her mum**, not herself.
She sees **people-facing** housing work as the place the three-year robot gap could help.

steps.text: Apply for paid retraining as a housing officer at the co-op
Find a cheaper flat with Anya before the job goes
Write to her MP every month about wage support
Join marches and push the union to negotiate early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them properly: retraining funds, a shorter working week, rules on what AI can sign off. I'd talk about it at the staff forum and online, though I'd try not to sound like a doom merchant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to change, but only just. Ruth would stop backfilling people when they leave, and by year three I'd be doing the work of two people with the AI's help. Then one day it'd be zero people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the AI training now and offer to be the person on my team who checks what it produces, because that's a job for a few years at least. I'd start a part-time course in social housing management in year two. And I'd put any pay rise straight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but busy. Being busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a part-time course cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a thousand a year, I think, and I haven't got it. I'd ask Hartfield to pay half, and if not, I'd pay monthly and cut the Friday dinners for good. Anya says she'll cook on Fridays instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one day it'd be zero people. When would you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to leave before the last round, not in it. Maybe year four. I'd rather walk out of Hartfield with a housing course finished than be the one my manager Ruth calls into the glass room.

say: Five years means **retraining funds**, a **shorter week** and rules on AI sign-off.
She'd raise it at the staff forum without sounding like a **doom merchant**.
think: Ruth would **stop backfilling** leavers until she's doing two people's work.
Five years is enough to change, but **only just**.
do: Take the AI training now and become the team's **AI checker**.
Start a part-time **social housing** management course in year two.
Put every **pay rise** straight into savings.
feel: Anxious but **busy**, and the busyness helps.
S3.quote: I'd rather walk out of Hartfield with a housing course finished than be the one my manager Ruth calls into the glass room.
fieldNote: Five years gives Bianca **some control**, so she plans her exit for around year four.
She'd use the transition role of **checking AI output** as a bridge.
Money is still the limit: a **thousand-pound course** depends on cutting Friday dinners.

steps.text: Volunteer as the charity team's checker of AI-drafted accounts
Enrol part-time in a social housing management course in year two
Pay every pay rise straight into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be idiots to waste it. Fund colleges, protect people mid-career, get unions into the planning. I'd say it at work, I'd say it in the pub, and I'd probably say it too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means I can actually choose. I'd be thirty-seven. I could move into housing or advice work properly, with time to build up experience before the robots come in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the AI training this year and keep the job while I study. I'd start volunteering at the housing co-op's tenant advice evenings, Tuesdays, to get experience. And I'd switch to a housing job by 2030, even if the pay dips at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still, because the money's thin and my job really does go. But it's a hopeful kind of anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a pay dip be possible on your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely. I'd need three months saved first, so I'd give myself until 2029 to get there. If Mum's health got worse, that plan would slip, and I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new graduate joining your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new graduate joining Hartfield to learn the numbers but build a career on the people, because the numbers are going and the people aren't.

say: Ten years is a **gift**: fund colleges and get **unions** into the planning.
She'd say it at work and in the pub, probably **too much**.
think: At thirty-seven she could **choose** a new direction.
There'd be time to build **housing experience** before robots arrive in 2039.
do: Volunteer at the co-op's **Tuesday tenant advice** evenings to gain experience.
Save **three months** of costs by 2029 before taking a pay dip.
feel: Still anxious because her **job goes**, but a **hopeful** kind of anxious.
S4.quote: I'd tell a new graduate joining Hartfield to learn the numbers but build a career on the people, because the numbers are going and the people aren't.
fieldNote: Even with ten years, Bianca expects her **accounting job to end**, so she stays anxious.
Her plan is **specific and dated**: volunteer now, save by 2029, switch by 2030.
Her **mum's health** is the one thing she knows could derail it.

steps.text: Volunteer at the housing co-op's Tuesday tenant advice evenings
Build three months of savings by 2029
Switch from charity accounts to a housing job by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd lose my job and my mum would lose her eighty pounds in the same month. What would help is being paid while I retrain, like a furlough, and a guarantee the co-op or the council could take people like me on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who does the charities' books after. A food bank can't afford an AI subscription and a human to check it. If small charities lose their accountant, the food bank treasurer ends up doing the books alone at midnight.

headlineQuote: If small charities lose their accountant, the food bank treasurer ends up doing the books alone at midnight.
portrait: Bianca is a **27-year-old** accountant at Hartfield Partners, doing year-end accounts for **charities** and co-ops.
She shares a flat with Anya and sends her **mum eighty a month**, leaving almost no savings.
She uses the firm's AI tool **now and then** and takes up training once it's proven.
She wants **shared gains**, union bargaining and paid retraining, and aims to move into **housing work**.
Her mood runs from uneasy in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when she'd lose her job and her mum's support money at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** like a furlough, plus a route into co-op or **council** jobs.
